title: Absorption, the Liver and Enterohepatic Circulation

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: For gut water, bile acids and first-pass drug loss, what rule links the residue to the load, and why is the residue so sensitive when capture is near complete?
cards.back: Residue = load × (1 − fraction captured). With capture near one, losing a few percentage points multiplies the residue; a bigger load at the same fraction raises it only in proportion.
cards.quote: What leaves is whatever was not taken back: residue = load × (1 − fraction captured).

cards.front: Of the 9 to 11 L a day entering the adult gut lumen, about {{c1::99 percent}} is reabsorbed.
cards.quote: give a load entering the lumen (the space inside the gut) of about 9 to 11 L a day, and about 99 percent of it is reabsorbed.
cards.section: Eleven litres in, about a tenth of a litre out

cards.front: An adult drinks 2.0 L a day and secretes 9.0 L a day into the gut. Overall reabsorption falls from 99 to 96 percent. What is stool water before and after?
cards.back: Load = 11.0 L a day. Before: 11.0 × 0.01 = 0.11 L a day. After: 11.0 × 0.04 = 0.44 L a day, four times as much.
cards.why: Near full capture, a three-point fall quadruples the unreabsorbed fraction.
cards.quote: It quadruples. Stool water = 11.0 × 0.04 = 0.44 L a day (check: 10.56 + 0.44 = 11.0 L).
cards.section: Eleven litres in, about a tenth of a litre out

cards.front: Why can a moderate rise in the fluid load reaching the gut leave stool water nearly unchanged?
cards.back: The colon can absorb up to 4 to 5 L a day, far more than usually reaches it, so the extra is soaked up with overall reabsorption still near 99 percent. Stool water climbs steeply only once that reserve is used up.
cards.quote: The colon can absorb up to 4 to 5 L a day, far more than usually reaches it
cards.section: Eleven litres in, about a tenth of a litre out

cards.front: How does a small-intestinal crypt cell secrete fluid into the lumen?
cards.back: The basolateral sodium pump and NKCC1 load chloride above equilibrium; apical CFTR lets it out. Sodium follows paracellularly to balance charge, and water follows by osmosis.
cards.quote: When CFTR opens, chloride rushes out into the lumen, sodium follows between the cells (the paracellular route) to balance the charge, and water follows both by osmosis.
cards.section: Crypts secrete, villi absorb, and the stool is the difference

cards.front: The apical chloride exit of intestinal crypt cells is {{c1::CFTR}}, regulated mainly by cyclic AMP- and cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinases.
cards.quote: Apical CFTR, a chloride channel regulated mainly by cyclic AMP- and cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinases, is the exit.
cards.section: Crypts secrete, villi absorb, and the stool is the difference

cards.front: How do NHE3 and a chloride/bicarbonate exchanger such as DRA together absorb sodium chloride on the villus without moving charge?
cards.back: NHE3 swaps luminal Na+ for cell H+; DRA swaps luminal Cl− for cell HCO3−. Each swap is like-for-like charge, so the net effect is NaCl into the cell; H+ and HCO3− form CO2 and water in the lumen.
cards.quote: Each swap is one ion for one of the same charge, so no charge moves
cards.section: Crypts secrete, villi absorb, and the stool is the difference

cards.front: In the {{c1::distal colon}}, sodium also enters epithelial cells electrogenically through ENaC.
cards.quote: In the distal colon sodium also enters electrogenically through ENaC.
cards.section: Crypts secrete, villi absorb, and the stool is the difference

cards.front: Ileal mucosa in an Ussing chamber is secreting chloride after a rise in cyclic AMP. Bumetanide, which blocks NKCC1, is added to the serosal bath. What happens to the secretory current, and why?
cards.back: It should fall, if the current depends on NKCC1 chloride loading: crypt chloride secretion relies on basolateral NKCC1 loading chloride into the cell above equilibrium; without that loading, opening CFTR has little chloride to release.
cards.quote: Test the messenger with bumetanide serosally, for whether the current depends on NKCC1 chloride loading
cards.section: Design problem (optional)

cards.front: How does cholera toxin keep cyclic AMP high in intestinal lining cells?
cards.back: It chemically modifies Gs so that Gs can no longer switch itself off; adenylyl cyclase stays on and keeps making cyclic AMP.
cards.quote: chemically modifies Gs, the G protein that turns on adenylyl cyclase, so that Gs can no longer switch itself off
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: In cholera, what does cyclic AMP do on the villi, and which term of stool water = load × (1 − fraction reabsorbed) does that move?
cards.back: It slows NHE3, so less sodium chloride and less water are absorbed: the fraction reabsorbed falls. (In the crypts it opens CFTR, raising the load.)
cards.quote: On the villi it slows NHE3. Less sodium chloride is absorbed, so less water follows it back.
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: With round illustrative numbers: cholera adds 5 L a day of secretion to a usual 11 L load, and overall reabsorption drops from 99 to 90 percent. How much does stool water change?
cards.back: Before: 11 × 0.01 = 0.11 L a day. After: 16 × 0.10 = 1.6 L a day, about fifteen times as much.
cards.why: Both terms move the wrong way at once, so their effects multiply.
cards.quote: Stool water goes from 11 × 0.01 = 0.11 L a day to 16 × 0.10 = 1.6 L a day, about fifteen times as much.
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: A sheet of rabbit ileum with no blood supply behind it is exposed to cholera toxin. It moves chloride toward the lumen, and its net sodium absorption falls to zero without reversing. What does this show about cholera fluid?
cards.back: The fluid is secreted by the epithelium itself, not leaking from the circulation through a damaged gut: there was no blood supply to leak from.
cards.quote: With toxin, the sheet itself moved chloride toward the lumen, and its net sodium absorption fell to zero but did not reverse
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: When cyclic AMP has slowed NHE3, why does adding luminal glucose bring sodium absorption back?
cards.back: Glucose enters through SGLT1, a different door that cyclic AMP does not shut. SGLT1 runs on the inward sodium gradient kept up by the basolateral pump, and water follows the absorbed solute.
cards.quote: Glucose enters through a different door, SGLT1, and cyclic AMP does not shut it.
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: SGLT1 carries {{c1::two}} sodium ions in with each glucose.
cards.quote: SGLT1 carries two sodium ions in with each glucose and runs on the inward sodium gradient the basolateral pump keeps up
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: The current reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution has {{c1::75 mmol}} each of sodium and glucose per litre.
cards.quote: The current reduced-osmolarity solution has 75 mmol of each per litre.
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: Does oral rehydration therapy stop cholera secretion? How does it work in terms of the residue rule?
cards.back: No. Secretion continues and stools can stay large; the drink raises the fraction reabsorbed through SGLT1, so the patient absorbs enough to keep pace.
cards.quote: The drink does not switch off secretion, and stools can stay large; it raises the fraction reabsorbed through SGLT1
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: A rehydration drink is made with far more glucose than the standard solution. Predict its effect on water absorption, and why.
cards.back: Extra glucose beyond what SGLT1 can carry stays in the lumen and holds water there by osmosis, so it stops helping and can hold water in the gut. That is why glucose and total concentration are kept moderate.
cards.quote: glucose beyond what SGLT1 can carry stays in the lumen and holds water there by osmosis
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: Intestine lacking functional apical CFTR is exposed to cholera toxin. Predict the change in the load term and in the fraction-reabsorbed term of stool water.
cards.back: By the lesson's mechanism, the load rise should be largely blunted: CFTR is the apical chloride exit that cyclic AMP opens, so little chloride, sodium and water should pour out. Cyclic AMP can still slow NHE3, so absorption may fall somewhat. Rests on: crypt secretion exits via CFTR.
cards.quote: In the crypts it opens CFTR. Chloride, sodium and water pour into the lumen, so the load goes up.
cards.section: Cholera, and why a sugar-and-salt drink works

cards.front: What do bile acid mixed micelles do in fat absorption, and what do they not do?
cards.back: They ferry lipolysis products across the watery unstirred layer next to the brush border; lipid molecules then leave the micelle one at a time and enter the cell. Micelles themselves do not cross the membrane.
cards.quote: The micelles ferry these products across the watery layer next to the brush border
cards.section: Fat takes the other door

cards.front: In the enterocyte, microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) assembles re-esterified lipid with newly made {{c1::apoB-48}} into chylomicrons.
cards.quote: microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) assembles the lipid with newly made apoB-48 into chylomicrons.
cards.section: Fat takes the other door

cards.front: Why does most long-chain dietary fat reach the blood through lymph rather than the portal vein?
cards.back: It leaves the enterocyte in chylomicrons, which are too large to enter blood capillaries. They enter the villus lacteal and travel the lymphatics to the thoracic duct, bypassing the liver's first pass.
cards.why: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids, sugars and amino acids do go to portal blood.
cards.quote: Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries.
cards.section: Fat takes the other door

cards.front: Intestinal biopsies show no MTP activity, as in abetalipoproteinemia. Predict what happens to long-chain fat absorbed into the enterocyte.
cards.back: Chylomicrons cannot be assembled, so long-chain fat cannot take its usual exit into the lacteal. Rests on: MTP packages lipid with apoB-48 into chylomicrons.
cards.quote: MTP activity was absent in intestinal biopsies from four people with abetalipoproteinemia.
cards.section: Proteins of fat uptake and packaging

cards.front: {{c1::CYP7A1}} is the rate-limiting enzyme of the classic pathway making bile acids from cholesterol in the liver.
cards.quote: CYP7A1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of the classic pathway from cholesterol.
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: Bile acid recovery is mostly active, through {{c1::ASBT}} in the terminal ileum.
cards.quote: Recovery is mostly active and mostly in one place: ASBT in the terminal ileum.
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: In the hepatocyte, which transporter carries most conjugated bile acid uptake from sinusoidal blood, and which is the major canalicular export pump?
cards.back: NTCP takes bile acids up; BSEP pumps them into bile.
cards.quote: Returning bile acids are removed efficiently in their first passage through the sinusoids, NTCP carrying most conjugated bile acid uptake.
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: How does the ileum put a brake on hepatic bile acid synthesis?
cards.back: Bile acids taken up by ileal ASBT activate the nuclear receptor FXR, which induces FGF19. FGF19 acts on the hepatocyte through FGFR4 with beta-klotho to lower CYP7A1.
cards.quote: Bile acids taken up by ileal ASBT activate FXR, a nuclear receptor (nuclear receptors), which induces FGF19.
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: A 3.5 g bile acid pool cycles 5 times a day, and measured fecal loss is 200 to 400 mg a day. Test the textbook figure of 95 percent reabsorption per cycle.
cards.back: Delivery = 3.5 × 5 = 17.5 g a day. Loss at 95 percent = 17.5 × 0.05 = 0.875 g a day, two to four times the measured loss, so 95 percent overstates loss.
cards.quote: 17.5 × 0.05 = 0.875 g a day, two to four times the measured 200 to 400 mg a day
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: Ileal bile acid recovery falls. When does the bile acid pool hold, and when does it shrink?
cards.back: The brake lifts and synthesis rises. If synthesis matches the extra loss, the pool holds; if not, the pool settles lower, at the size where loss equals synthesis.
cards.quote: If it does not, the pool settles lower, at the size where loss equals synthesis.
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: Ileal disease cuts bile acid reabsorption to 90 percent per cycle at 5 cycles a day, and suppose (illustratively) the liver can raise synthesis only to 0.6 g a day. Where does the pool settle, and what follows for fat absorption at an ordinary fat load?
cards.back: Pool = synthesis ÷ (cycles × (1 − f)) = 0.6 ÷ (5 × 0.10) = 1.2 g, about a third of 3.5 g. Fewer bile acids for micelles, so steatorrhea can join the diarrhea.
cards.why: Rests on the steady-state rule synthesis = loss, rearranged for the pool.
cards.quote: so the same rule, rearranged, gives pool = synthesis ÷ (cycles × (1 − fraction reabsorbed))
cards.section: A pool used five times a day

cards.front: A drug partly blocks ASBT (a mild block). Predict FGF19, CYP7A1, synthesis, the pool and the stool.
cards.back: FGF19 falls, the brake on CYP7A1 lifts and synthesis rises, so the pool holds. More bile acid reaches the colon, where it induces fluid secretion: diarrhea, but enough bile acid for micelles.
cards.quote: Less bile acid enters ileal cells, so FGF19 falls, the brake on CYP7A1 lifts and synthesis rises.
cards.section: Lesion problem: block ileal uptake

cards.front: Passive absorption along the whole intestine might replace the ileal transporter. Mice lacking ASBT show fecal bile acid up 10- to 20-fold and a pool about 80 percent smaller despite more synthesis. What does this show?
cards.back: ASBT is needed for efficient bile acid absorption; alternative routes cannot compensate for its loss. Had they taken over, the pool would have stayed roughly intact.
cards.quote: fecal bile acid excretion rose 10- to 20-fold and the pool fell by about 80 percent despite increased synthesis
cards.section: Lesion problem: block ileal uptake

cards.front: In a fasting adult at rest, about {{c1::75 percent}} of hepatic blood flow arrives by the portal vein, the rest by the hepatic artery.
cards.back: A textbook figure; measured values vary, and portal flow rises after a meal.
cards.quote: About 75 percent of hepatic blood flow arrives by the portal vein and about 25 percent by the hepatic artery
cards.section: The liver as the first organ downstream

cards.front: Define the hepatic extraction ratio E_H and systemic availability F, and state how they relate for a completely absorbed drug with no gut-wall metabolism.
cards.back: E_H is the fraction removed in one passage through the liver (first pass); F is the fraction that gets through. F = 1 − E_H.
cards.quote: The hepatic extraction ratio, E_H, is the fraction removed in one passage through the liver (the first pass)
cards.section: The liver as the first organ downstream

cards.front: Why is a hepatic extraction ratio calculated as 1 − F from a measured oral availability only an upper bound?
cards.back: Incomplete absorption or loss in the gut wall would also lower F, so not all of the missing fraction can be assigned to the liver unless those conditions are verified.
cards.quote: If they are unverified, these values are only upper bounds, because loss in the gut would also lower F.
cards.section: The liver as the first organ downstream

cards.front: A drug has E_H = 0.8. In liver disease, 30 percent of portal blood bypasses the liver through a portosystemic shunt (E_H itself unchanged). What is oral availability before and after?
cards.back: Before: F = 1 − 0.8 = 0.20. After: F = 0.3 + 0.7 × 0.2 = 0.44, about 2.2-fold higher.
cards.why: Only blood that passes the liver loses drug; high-extraction drugs sit at the rule's sensitive end.
cards.quote: Only the 70 percent that passes the liver loses anything; the 30 percent that skips it all survives
cards.section: The liver as the first organ downstream

cards.front: Healthy people fast for 68 hours. Liver glycogen is followed by carbon-13 NMR and whole-body glucose production by a labelled tracer. How is gluconeogenesis obtained, and what share of production does it supply by about 22 hours?
cards.back: Gluconeogenesis = total production − measured glycogen breakdown. It supplied 64 percent by about 22 hours, then 82 and 96 percent later: the two sources overlap rather than run in sequence.
cards.quote: Gluconeogenesis supplied 64 percent of production by about 22 hours, then 82 and 96 percent in the following 14 and 18 hours.
cards.section: Glucose output in a fast

cards.front: Name the hepatic steps for bilirubin from blood to bile and the enzyme or transporter for the last two.
cards.back: Uptake from blood, conjugation by UGT1A1 with glucuronic acid, and export into bile by transporters including MRP2.
cards.quote: UGT1A1 conjugates it with glucuronic acid, transporters including MRP2 export the conjugate into bile
cards.section: Bilirubin: the step that fails names what rises

cards.front: Heme breakdown during hemolysis outruns hepatic conjugating capacity. Which bilirubin rises in blood, and does it appear in urine?
cards.back: Unconjugated bilirubin rises, and it does not appear in urine, because albumin-bound bilirubin is not filtered in free form.
cards.quote: Albumin-bound bilirubin is not filtered in free form
cards.section: Bilirubin: the step that fails names what rises

cards.front: A stone obstructs bile flow. Predict blood bilirubin, urine bilirubin, and urobilinogen and stool pigment.
cards.back: Conjugated bilirubin rises in blood and appears in urine, because the conjugate is water soluble. Less conjugate reaches the gut, so urobilinogen and stool pigment fall.
cards.quote: When bile flow is blocked, less conjugate reaches the gut, so urobilinogen and stool pigment fall
cards.section: Bilirubin: the step that fails names what rises

cards.front: Bile flow is blocked for weeks. Besides the bilirubin change, predict what happens to absorption of long-chain dietary fat, and name the rules you combined.
cards.back: Fat absorption should fall at an ordinary fat load: bile acids are sent into bile and are needed to form micelles, so with bile blocked fewer reach the lumen. Bilirubin rule: export failure raises conjugated bilirubin.
cards.quote: Export: loss of MRP2, or obstruction of bile flow
cards.section: Bilirubin: the step that fails names what rises

cards.front: Before Ussing-chamber studies, what measurement on cholera stool already argued against fluid filtering through a damaged lining?
cards.back: Clearance of mannitol, a small paracellular probe, into the stool was very low, which is not what a leaky barrier would give.
cards.quote: clearance of small molecules such as mannitol, a paracellular probe, into the stool was found to be very low, which already made filtration untenable
cards.section: The Field experiment in detail

cards.front: A sealed litre holds 75 mmol of sodium and 75 mmol of a sugar carried by SGLT1, with no sodium coming in. What is the most sugar SGLT1 can move?
cards.back: SGLT1 couples 2 Na+ per sugar, so 75 ÷ 2 = 37.5 mmol of sugar. In the gut, sodium is resupplied and is not the limiting partner.
cards.quote: with no sodium coming in, 75 mmol of sodium can carry only 37.5 mmol of sugar through SGLT1
cards.section: Sodium–glucose stoichiometry

cards.front: In an Ussing chamber, a bacterial filtrate raises the serosa-to-mucosa chloride flux. Why is that alone not proof of active chloride secretion, and what result would rule it in?
cards.back: A one-way flux can also rise through a leakier junction. Active anion secretion is ruled in by a net secretory chloride flux at zero voltage with identical solutions on both sides, and unchanged mannitol flux.
cards.quote: A rise in serosa-to-mucosa chloride flux alone is not enough, since a one-way flux can also rise through a leakier junction.
cards.section: Design problem (optional)

cards.front: You add glucose to the mucosal bath of filtrate-treated ileum to ask whether sodium-coupled absorption survives. What control is needed, and what does it separate?
cards.back: A non-transported sugar at the same concentration. It separates an osmotic effect of adding sugar from true sodium-glucose cotransport through SGLT1.
cards.quote: with a non-transported sugar at the same concentration as the control separating an osmotic effect from cotransport
cards.section: Design problem (optional)
